title: Why riding faster gets you more red lights
description:
On a green wave, each light turns green a fixed time after the one before: here 45 seconds for 250 metres, the time a bike needs at 20 km/h. Ride at 20 and you meet every one of ten lights at the same point in its green. Ride at 30 and you gain 15 seconds a block, run into a red within a light or two, and from then on wait about 15 seconds at every light: at least nine stops, and you arrive at most 30 seconds sooner (it would be 2.5 minutes with no lights). Copenhagen runs a green wave like this for cyclists at about 20 km/h over 2.5 km.

Numbers checked in code (the ride timed light by light, plus 200,000 simulated rides from random points in the green). Example road: 10 lights, 250 m apart, 60 s cycle, 30 s green. Source: Wikipedia, Green wave.

social_caption: Ride at 20 and every light is green. Ride at 30 and you stop at nine of them. Here's how a green wave decides when you get home.
facts_checked: Example road: 10 lights 250 m apart (2.5 km), 60 s cycle, 30 s green, offset 45 s = 250 m at 20 km/h; at 20 km/h 0 stops and 7.5 min from any point in the green; at 30 km/h 30 s per block, 15 s gained per block, 9 or 10 stops (average 9.5), 15 s wait at each, time saved = how far into the green you started, always under 30 s (average 15); no lights: 7.5 vs 5 min = 2.5 min (verify.py, 200,000 simulated rides)
A green wave: lights share one cycle, each offset by distance / platoon speed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_wave)
Copenhagen: a green wave on Norrebrogade lets cyclists keep about 20 km/h over 2.5 km (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_wave)

beats.say: Pedal at 20, all greens. Pedal faster, nine reds.
It's not bad luck, and you're not too slow. These lights are set for exactly one speed.
Your road has 10 lights, 250 meters apart. Each turns green 45 seconds after the one before. That's how long 250 meters takes at 20.
So pedal at 20. You meet every light at the same moment of its green. Zero stops, all the way.
Now pedal at 30. Each block takes 30 seconds, not 45. You gain 15 seconds every block, and soon the next light is still red.
So you wait. You sprint. And you catch the next red.
You're stuck at the front of the wave, waiting 15 seconds at every light.
With no lights, 30 would save you two and a half minutes. Here it saves under 30 seconds. The lights decide when you get home. Copenhagen runs one for bikes at 20, for 2.5 kilometers.
